newsitem.title: USA: Budget amendment would hit social security - Dems.
newsitem.headline: Budget amendment would hit social security - Dems.

text.p: Democrats warned on Wednesday that the solvency of Social Security would be in jeopardy early next century if the Republican version of a balanced budget amendment was adopted.
Republicans responded that only the discipline of a U.S. constitutional requirement to keep federal spending in check could save the retirement system.

The fight over whether Social Security should be exempt from the balanced budget amendment could determine whether Republicans muster the two-thirds vote necessary to carry the measure in the House and Senate. Leaders of both parties said this week the vote was too close to call.

Senate Democrats plan to offer several proposals to keep the rising Social Security trust funds from being used to offset other government spending. Without that protection, they fear the money would not be available to pay benefits in the next century.

But Senate Finance Committee chairman William Roth, a Delaware Republican, told reporters the issue was being raised as a way to defeat the balanced budget amendment. "It is a rationale not to vote for it," he said.

Roth and other Republicans argued that only by mandating the budget be balanced would Congress and the White House make the hard choices necessary to cut spending and end budget deficits. The budget was last balanced in 1969.

Senate Judiciary Committee chairman Orrin Hatch, a Utah Republican, said Congress would have to address long-term problems of Social Security anyway. If the budget were balanced, that job would be easier because the economy would be stronger.

"The only way we will gather the courage and discipline to address our budgetary problems is if we have a constitutional requirement to balance the federal budget," he said during the lengthy Senate debate. The issue will flare up when the Senate nears a final vote at the end of the month.

President Clinton wants Social Security taken out of the balanced budget amendment, an idea that has gained backing in the House, particularly among a group of Republicans who disagree with their party leaders. House Judiciary Committee chairman Henry Hyde, an Illinois Republican, postponed indefinitely the vote on the balanced budget amendment when it appeared the Social Security change would win.

The constitutional amendment would require the federal government balance its budget each year during peacetime. It would make it more difficult for Congress to approve deficit spending, raise taxes or borrow money. If passed by two-thirds of the House and Senate it would have to be ratified by 38 of 50 states, a process that could take up to seven years.
The amendment passed the House in 1995 but failed in the Senate by one vote.

Democrats Byron Dorgan and Kent Conrad of North Dakota and Harry Reid of Nevada on Wednesday released a new report from the Congressional Research Service which said the Social Security system's financial problems will begin in 2020 if the constitutional amendment is passed, 10 years earlier than other estimates. They will offer the key proposals to change the constitutional amendment.

"The Republican amendment is a time-bomb for baby-boomers," Dorgan said. It would bar the government from borrowing money to pay debts, including Social Security benefits, unless three-fifths of the Congress agreed.
Dorgan said massive tax increases or cuts in federal spending would be needed to pay retirement benefits.

Social Security benefits for the 38 million retirees and disabled persons consume 22 percent of annual federal spending. Currently, the amount employers and workers contribute in payroll taxes more than meets this cost.
